title: Breathing, alone
tomorrow: someone digs at you with words. how can a mind be like the earth?

lines: IN FOR FOUR, HOLD FOR SEVEN.
BREATHING IN LONG, YOU KNOW IT.
STEER IT, OR ONLY WATCH IT?
cards: Breathing apps love a count. In for four, hold for seven, out for eight. A circle swells and shrinks and you follow it.
Then you read MN 118 through on your own, and the first lines say something different. Breathing in long, you know: i breathe in long. Breathing in short, you know: i breathe in short.
Not make it long. Know it. So which is it: steer the breath, or only watch it?

teach.b: MN 118 lays the practice out as steps, in four sets of four. Body: knowing long breaths, knowing short ones, feeling the whole body, calming it.

Feelings: breathing with joy, with ease, with the mind's movements, calming them. Mind: knowing the mind, gladdening it, steadying it, freeing it. And last: watching impermanence, fading, ending, letting go.
Here the tradition has two honest readings. One view holds to the opening verb.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: KNOW IT, DON'T MANAGE IT.
teach.b: You know the breath; you don't manage it. Control smuggles in the very wanting the practice is meant to see through, so let the breath be whatever it is and keep knowing. The other view points at the later steps.
From the third on, the sutta says you train: i will breathe in calming the body.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: 'YOU TRAIN' MEANS SOME SHAPING.

teach.b: So some teachers start with a few deliberate slow breaths to settle, then let go of steering. Each side has the text.
The first trusts that knowing is enough to calm. The second trusts that a little guidance at the start is part of the training. Both end in the same place: letting go.

how: Mindfulness of breathing (anapanasati) is taught across Buddhist traditions; teachers differ on whether to let the breath be entirely natural or to begin with a few deliberate slow breaths.

mindfulness of breath laid out in steps, start to end
breath exercises monks do before they chant

games.q: the four sets in MN 118 — tap the pairs.
p: joy, ease, calming the mind's movements

s: MN 118 begins by telling you to breathe in for a set count
it begins with knowing: breathing in long, you know you breathe in long.
the sutta uses 'you train' for many of the later steps
that's why some teachers allow a little gentle shaping at the start.
breath meditation stops at calming the body
the steps go on through feelings and mind to watching impermanence and letting go.

games.q: your friend says breath meditation is pointless unless you count and hold. give each view its best case.
o: one: just knowing the breath lets it calm. two: a little gentle shaping helps you start.
counting is the only real method; the sutta just forgot to mention it
breathing is automatic, so there's nothing to practice at all
games.why: both readings have the text: the opening steps say 'you know', the later ones say 'you train'. teachers differ, and both end in letting go.

practice: Take the first four steps only. Know the long breaths as long and the short ones as short. Then feel the whole body breathing, and on each out-breath let it soften a little, without forcing anything.

wordCard.voice: Breathing: in MN 118, mindfulness of breathing laid out as sixteen steps, from knowing a long breath to letting go.

orig.note: Pali: mindfulness (sati) of breathing in and out (anapana). MN 118 is the Anapanasati Sutta.

carryVoice: Sixteen steps, and the first is just knowing a breath is long. See you tomorrow.
